meta.blurb: In a lecture hall in London, Michael Faraday lit one ordinary candle and used it to explain fire, air, water and even breathing. Sit among his young audience and see how much a small flame can teach you.
meta.bible: Michael Faraday: English scientist, born in 1791 in London, the son of a blacksmith. He left school young, was apprenticed to a bookbinder, read the books he bound, and became assistant to Humphry Davy. The Royal Institution: a scientific society in London where Faraday worked. He gave its Christmas Lectures for young people; he gave his series on The Chemical History of a Candle at Christmas 1848, and again in 1860 and 1861. The book: six lectures, printed in 1861 from notes taken by William Crookes. Lecture titles in order: A Candle, Brightness of Flame, Products of Combustion, Hydrogen in the Candle, Oxygen and the Air, Carbon and Breathing. The experiments: a Candle, Wick, Tallow, Beeswax, Spermaceti, Capillary attraction, Vapour, Davy's safety lamp and Wire gauze, the Argand burner and Chimney, Soot, Camphor, Turpentine, Ice and salt freezing mixture, Potassium, Battery and Electricity, Hydrogen, Oxygen, Chlorate of potash, Manganese, Nitrogen, Atmosphere, Pressure, Limewater, Carbonic acid (the old name of carbon dioxide, which this book calls Carbon dioxide), Charcoal, Carbon, Coal gas, Respiration, Combustion, Compound, Particles. Everything in this book is a real demonstration of Faraday's or a plain fact of chemistry; no number is invented. Voice: warm, clear and curious, like Faraday speaking to children; one small flame leads to the biggest ideas.

beats.scene: A lecture hall full of children watching a man light a candle
beats.summary: Lecture 1: at the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday lights one candle in front of a young audience.

beats.scene: A young bookbinder reads a book at his bench by candlelight
beats.summary: Faraday was born into a poor family, became a bookbinder's apprentice, read the books he bound, and rose to be a great scientist.

beats.scene: Candles of yellow tallow, pale wax and white fat in a row
beats.summary: Faraday shows candles made of different materials: tallow, beeswax, and some made from whale oil, and newer kinds.

beats.scene: A lit candle with a small clear pool of melted wax around its flame
beats.summary: When a candle is lit, the heat melts the wax around the wick and makes a little cup of liquid.

beats.scene: A candle in a draught with wax running down one side of it
beats.summary: A steady flow of air cools the edge of the candle so the cup stays whole, but in a draught the wax runs down one side.

beats.scene: Wax climbs up a wick in a close picture, drawn with little arrows
beats.summary: The liquid wax climbs up the wick by capillary attraction, the way water climbs through a sponge.

beats.scene: A sponge and a towel dipping into water, with the water climbing up
beats.summary: The same thing happens when a sponge or the corner of a towel dips in water and the water climbs up into it.

beats.scene: A blown-out candle with a trail of smoke and a taper above it
beats.summary: When the candle is blown out, a thin trail of vapour rises, and a flame brought near it jumps down and relights the candle.

beats.scene: A bent glass tube carries vapour from a flame to a second flame
beats.summary: With a bent glass tube, Faraday draws vapour from the dark middle of the flame and lights it at the other end of the tube.

beats.scene: A candle flame pressed against a fine wire gauze that stops it rising
beats.summary: A fine wire gauze held over a flame stops the fire from passing through, which is how Davy's safety lamp for miners works.

beats.scene: A flame in a tall glass chimney burns steady beside one that flickers
beats.summary: In a lamp with a chimney, a draught of air feeds the flame so that it burns steady and bright.

beats.scene: A tall pointed flame with arrows showing hot air rising around it
beats.summary: A flame is shaped like a tongue because the hot gas around it rises upward.

beats.scene: Tiny glowing specks inside a yellow flame, drawn very large
beats.summary: Faraday explains that a candle flame shines because of tiny solid particles of carbon that glow white hot.

beats.scene: A cold white plate held in a flame and covered with black soot
beats.summary: If a cold plate is held in the flame, it is covered with black soot, which is the carbon that was glowing.

beats.scene: A smoky flame throws up black clouds of soot above a small dish
beats.summary: Some flames, such as those of camphor and turpentine, give off thick smoke because they cannot burn all their carbon.

beats.scene: A clean-burning candle flame with no smoke rising from it
beats.summary: A candle burns without smoke because the carbon is burned up completely and turns into an invisible gas.

beats.scene: A candle burning under a glass jar, with the flame growing small and dim
beats.summary: When a glass jar is put over a burning candle, the flame grows dim and goes out after a short time.

beats.scene: Two candles in two bottles, one open and bright, one corked and low
beats.summary: A candle burns well in an open bottle but not in a closed one: it needs a steady supply of fresh air.

beats.scene: A cold glass beaker above a flame, covered with drops of water
beats.summary: When a very cold vessel is held over a flame, drops of water gather on its outside.

beats.scene: A small piece of metal bursts into a lilac flame on water
beats.summary: Faraday proves it is water by dropping the metal potassium on it, which bursts into flame the way it does on any water.

beats.scene: A block of ice, a glass of water and a steaming kettle
beats.summary: Water is the same stuff as ice or steam, and Faraday shows all three of its forms.

beats.scene: Two glass tubes with bubbles rising from two wires connected to a battery
beats.summary: Faraday passes electricity through water and splits it into two gases, one of which has twice the volume of the other.

beats.scene: A soap bubble full of a light gas rises toward a lecture hall ceiling
beats.summary: Next, one of the two gases from water is hydrogen, the lightest of all gases, which lifts soap bubbles into the air.

beats.scene: A pale, nearly invisible flame burns at the top of a small glass tube
beats.summary: Hydrogen burns with a pale flame that gives almost no light, and the only thing it makes is water.

beats.scene: A candle with a picture of tiny hydrogen and carbon pieces inside the wax
beats.summary: The wax of a candle contains hydrogen as well as carbon, and the hydrogen burns into the water that Faraday collected.

beats.scene: A glass flask over a flame, with gas bubbling through water into a jar
beats.summary: The other gas in water is oxygen, which Faraday makes by heating a white powder with a black one.

beats.scene: A candle blazes with a brilliant white flame inside a jar of pure oxygen
beats.summary: A candle burns far more brightly in pure oxygen than in air, and a piece of charcoal glows fiercely.

beats.scene: A bottle of air divided into five parts, with one part coloured
beats.summary: The air around us is a mixture of gases, and about one fifth of it is oxygen.

beats.scene: A glass bell jar on a table, with a pump beside it
beats.summary: Faraday shows that air has weight and presses on everything, with about a kilogram on each square centimetre.

beats.scene: A calm grey gas in a jar where a burning match is put out
beats.summary: Nitrogen, the other part of the air, does not burn or help burning, and it keeps the oxygen from burning things too fast.

beats.scene: Clear limewater turning milky white as a gas from a candle bubbles through it
beats.summary: The second thing a candle makes is an invisible gas, which turns clear limewater milky, now called carbon dioxide.

beats.scene: A piece of charcoal burns red in a jar and clear limewater turns white
beats.summary: Charcoal, which is nearly pure carbon, burns into the same gas, so the gas comes from the carbon in the candle.

beats.scene: An invisible gas is poured down a channel onto a row of candle flames
beats.summary: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, and Faraday pours the invisible gas down a trough to put out a row of candles.

beats.scene: A candle burns on a table and little arrows show gases rising away
beats.summary: Nothing in a candle is lost: it all turns into invisible water vapour and carbon dioxide that go into the air.

beats.scene: A piece of red glowing charcoal with no flame at all above it
beats.summary: Lecture 6: carbon in the form of charcoal burns without any flame, because it does not turn to vapour first.

beats.scene: A clay pipe full of coal, sealed with clay, with a small flame
beats.summary: Heated coal gives off a gas that burns like a candle's vapour, and this is the gas used to light towns.

beats.scene: Gas street lamps glowing along a London street at dusk
beats.summary: The lamps that light the streets burn coal gas, so they are really the same as a candle with a different fuel.

beats.scene: A boy blows through a glass tube into limewater that turns milky
beats.summary: Faraday breathes through a tube into limewater, and it turns milky white, just as it did for the candle.

beats.scene: A girl eats bread and an apple, beside a drawing of lungs
beats.summary: The reason: the food we eat is a kind of fuel, and in the body it combines slowly with the oxygen we breathe in.

beats.scene: A child wraps her hands around a warm mug beside a candle flame
beats.summary: This slow burning in the body gives us warmth, so we are a little like a slow, gentle candle.

beats.scene: A green plant in sunlight with small arrows bringing gas into its leaves
beats.summary: Plants take in carbon dioxide from the air and use its carbon to grow, so the gas from candles and breath is food for plants.

beats.scene: A candle, a flower and a child's face shown inside one large circle
beats.summary: Faraday says that the same laws govern a candle, a plant and a person, and nature is one connected whole.

beats.scene: A boy looks closely at a flame through a magnifying glass
beats.summary: Faraday asks the children to look carefully, to ask questions and to trust only what they have tested.

beats.scene: A child lights a small candle at a kitchen table beside a parent
beats.summary: Anyone can repeat many of Faraday's experiments with a candle, a plate and a jar, if an adult is helping them.

beats.scene: Faraday at a long table with a lamp, looking at a row of notebooks
beats.summary: Faraday says that the candle has taught only the first small lessons, and much remains for them to discover.

beats.scene: Faraday closes the last lecture while a row of lit candles glows before him
beats.summary: At the end of the last lecture, Faraday wishes that the children will grow up to be like candles, giving light to those around them.

beats.scene: A printed book about a candle lies open on a school desk
beats.summary: The lectures were printed as a book in 1861, written down from notes by William Crookes, and have been read ever since.

beats.scene: Faraday in his laboratory with magnets and coils of copper wire
beats.summary: Faraday also made great discoveries about electricity, including the principle behind the electric generator and motor.

beats.scene: A small flame reflected in a child's wide curious eyes
beats.summary: Faraday shows that the smallest everyday things can lead to the biggest ideas if we look carefully enough.

beats.scene: A single candle burning in a dark window at night, with the stars above
beats.summary: Next time you light a candle, you can see what Faraday saw: the cup, the wick, the vapour, the glow and the invisible gases.

B1B2: In a lecture hall at the Royal Institution in London, Michael Faraday placed a single candle on his table. He told the children in front of him that this simple thing was a door to all of nature.
Faraday had been a poor boy, who left school early to work for a bookbinder. He read the books he was binding, and his curiosity took him all the way to the Royal Institution.
Faraday began by showing his audience different candles, some old and some new. They were made of animal fat, of beeswax from bees, of a waxy oil from whales, and of newer materials.
When you light a candle, the heat of the flame melts the wax around the wick. The melted wax gathers in a little cup at the top of the candle, and the flame sits above it.
The cup forms because the air flowing upward cools the outside edge of the candle, so the edge stays solid. In a draught the air moves unevenly, and the cup is spoiled, so the wax runs down the side.
How does the melted wax get up to the flame? It climbs up through the wick, which is made of many tiny threads, and this movement is called capillary attraction.
You can see the same thing at home with a towel. If one corner dips into water, the water slowly climbs up into the dry part, because of the tiny spaces between the threads.
Faraday blew out a candle and held a lighted taper in the white trail of smoke above it. The flame ran down the trail and lit the wick again, which showed that the smoke was really burning fuel.

Faraday put a bent glass tube into the middle of the flame and found that vapour came out of the other end. He lit it, and a second small flame burned there, so the dark middle of a flame is full of unburned vapour.
Faraday held a fine wire gauze over a flame and showed that the fire did not pass through it. The metal takes away the heat, and this idea was used in Davy's safety lamp for coal miners.
Faraday lit a special lamp, called an Argand burner, with a glass chimney around it. The chimney made a steady stream of fresh air flow up to the flame, so it burned strongly, with no flicker.
Faraday explained why a flame is pointed at the top. The hot air around it is lighter, so it rises, and it carries the flame upward into the shape of a tongue.
Why is a candle flame so bright, and what makes it shine? Faraday said that it is full of tiny pieces of solid carbon, too small to see, and the heat makes them glow.
To prove it, Faraday held a cold white plate in the flame. It quickly became covered with black soot, which is the same carbon that had been glowing, and it was now cooled and caught.
Some materials, such as camphor and turpentine, burn with a very smoky flame. The black smoke is carbon that did not have enough air to burn, so it floats up and falls as soot.
A good candle makes no smoke at all, because it burns its carbon completely. The carbon pieces burn away at the edge of the flame, where they meet the air, and become an invisible gas.
Faraday placed a glass jar over a burning candle. At first it burned well, but soon the flame grew weak and died, because it had used up something that it needed.
A candle in an open bottle kept burning well, but one in a closed bottle soon went out. Faraday used this to show that fire needs fresh air, and that air which has been used is no good.
Next, Faraday held a very cold vessel, filled with ice and salt, above a flame. Drops of liquid soon formed on the outside of it, and when he collected them, they proved to be pure water.
To prove that the liquid really was water, Faraday used the metal potassium. When a small piece is dropped on water, it bursts into flame, and it did exactly this on the drops from the candle.
Faraday reminded his audience that ice, water and steam are all the same substance in different forms. Cold turns water into ice, and heat turns it into steam, but it is the same water throughout.
Faraday connected two wires from a battery to a dish of water. Bubbles of gas rose from the wires and were collected in two tubes, and one tube filled with twice as much gas as the other.
One of the two gases from water is called hydrogen, and it is the lightest gas of all. Faraday filled soap bubbles with it, and they floated up toward the ceiling, while ordinary bubbles sank.
Faraday lit the hydrogen, and it burned with a very pale flame that gave almost no light. It made no smoke or soot, and the only thing it made was water, which collected on a cold glass above it.
Faraday explained that the wax of a candle contains hydrogen as well as carbon. When the wax burns, the hydrogen joins with something in the air to make the water that he had caught.
Now Faraday turned to the other gas in water, which is called oxygen. He made some by heating a mixture of two powders in a glass flask, and he collected the gas in a jar over water.

Faraday lowered a burning candle into a jar of oxygen, and the flame burst into a brilliant light. A piece of charcoal glowed much more brightly in it, too, which showed that oxygen makes things burn faster.
Faraday explained that the air around us is a mixture of gases, and oxygen is only one part of it. Roughly one fifth of the air is oxygen, and the rest is mostly another gas.
Faraday also showed that air has weight, although it seems like nothing. The whole sky above us presses down on everything, with about as much force as a kilogram on each square centimetre.

Most of the air is nitrogen, a gas that does not burn and does not help other things to burn. Faraday said it works as a quiet friend, because it stops the oxygen from making everything burn too fast.
A candle makes a second thing besides water, and Faraday found it with limewater. The gas from a burning candle turns clear limewater white and milky, and this gas is now called carbon dioxide.
Faraday burned some charcoal, which is almost pure carbon, in a jar of oxygen. The gas it made also turned limewater white, so the gas from a candle is made from carbon.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, and Faraday showed this by pouring it from a jar. The gas flowed down a sloping trough over a row of lit candles, and they went out one after another.
When a candle burns away, nothing is truly lost. All of the wax becomes water vapour and carbon dioxide, which are invisible gases that go up into the air.
In the last lecture, Faraday spoke about carbon in the form of charcoal. Charcoal burns with a red glow but no flame, because it does not first turn into a vapour as candle wax does.
Faraday filled a clay pipe with coal and closed it with clay. When he heated it, a gas came out of the end, and when he lit it, it burned just like the vapour of a candle.
The lamps in the streets of London burned gas that came from coal. Faraday said they were really the same as a candle, because both burn a gas with a bright flame, and only the fuel is different.
Then Faraday did something surprising with a glass tube. He blew through it into clear limewater, and the water turned white and milky, exactly as it had for the gas from a candle.
Faraday explained the reason: food is a kind of fuel. In our bodies it is slowly joined with the oxygen we breathe in, and we breathe out the carbon dioxide that results.
This slow burning is what keeps our bodies warm, even on a cold day. A candle burns fast and hot, and our bodies burn their food slowly and gently, but the same kind of change goes on in both.
Plants take in the carbon dioxide that we and candles make. They use the carbon to build their leaves and stems, so the gas that we breathe out helps the green plants to grow.
Faraday said that the same laws of nature work in a candle and in a living person. He wanted the children to see that nature is one connected whole, and not a lot of separate parts.
Faraday asked the children to look carefully and to ask questions about everything. He said they should believe only what they had tested themselves, and not simply take someone else's word for it.
Many of Faraday's experiments are simple, and children can try some of them at home with a grown-up to help. A candle, a cold plate and a glass jar are enough to show a good deal.
Faraday was modest about all this, and he said that a candle had much more to teach. The children had only begun to learn, and there was still a great deal in nature that nobody understood.
At the end of the last lecture, Faraday made a wish for the children. He hoped that, when they grew up, they would be like candles and give light to everyone around them.

The lectures were printed as a book in 1861, based on notes taken by a young scientist named William Crookes. It has stayed popular with readers and teachers ever since, and has been read in many countries.
Faraday was famous for many other discoveries, too, such as how magnets and moving wire can make electricity. This is the idea behind the electric motors and generators that we use today.
The great lesson of the lectures is that small, ordinary things can lead to the biggest ideas, if we look carefully enough. A candle on a table can teach us about air, water, fire and even life.
The next time you see a candle burning, remember what Faraday showed. Look at the cup of wax, the wick, the bright glow and the pale edge, and think of the invisible gases drifting away.
C1C2: In a crowded lecture hall at the Royal Institution in London, the scientist Michael Faraday set a single candle on the table before an audience of eager young people. He told them, with the confidence of a man who had studied it for many years, that there was no better door into the study of nature than the burning of a candle. Every law that governs the universe, he promised, is somewhere to be found in that small flame.

Faraday had not been born to wealth, for his father was a blacksmith, and at the age of fourteen he was apprenticed to a bookbinder. He read the books he was asked to bind, went to lectures by Humphry Davy, and sent Davy a book of his own careful notes, which so impressed the great man that he took him on as an assistant. From that humble position he rose, by sheer curiosity and hard work, to be one of the great scientists of his century.

Faraday began by showing his audience a collection of candles, old and new, laid out in a row upon the table. Some were made from tallow, which is animal fat, some from the beeswax that bees make, some from a waxy oil taken from whales, and some from newer materials that had been invented in his own lifetime. Whatever they were made of, he said, they all burned in much the same way.

When a candle is first lit, the heat of the flame melts the solid wax around the wick, and the liquid gathers in a small and very beautiful cup at the top. Faraday pointed out that this cup holds the fuel of the flame, kept ready for use in just the right place. It is, he said, a most elegant arrangement, and he asked the audience to notice it every time they lit a candle.

The cup keeps its shape because a gentle current of rising air cools the outer edge of the candle and keeps it from melting. When a draught blows the flame to one side, the current becomes uneven, the rim melts away and the liquid wax runs down the side of the candle in a wasteful stream. A good candle therefore needs still air, said Faraday, and a careful hand to guard it.

How does the fuel travel from the cup up to the flame, against gravity? Faraday explained that the liquid wax creeps up the wick through the tiny spaces between its threads, in a way called capillary attraction. The wick carries it steadily upward and delivers it to the heat in exactly the quantity that the flame can use.

Faraday showed that this climbing of liquids is a common thing, and he reminded his audience of how water rises into a sponge, or into the corner of a towel that has been left in a basin. In each case the liquid is drawn through very narrow spaces by a force that acts between the liquid and the material. The wick of a candle is simply a clever use of the same principle.

To show what really burns in a candle, Faraday blew out the flame and quickly held a burning taper in the pale stream of vapour that rose from the wick. The fire leapt down the stream, some distance from the wick, and relit the candle with a little flash, which proved that what burns is not the solid wax but the vapour that rises from it. The heat of the flame first turns the melted wax into a gas, and the gas is what we see burning.

Faraday thrust one end of a bent glass tube into the dark centre of the flame, and from the far end of the tube, to the surprise of the audience, there came out a white vapour that would burn. When he lit it, a second small flame stood at the end of the tube, burning quite happily, though it was some distance from the candle. The middle of a flame, he explained, is full of vapour that has not yet found enough air to burn.

Faraday held a piece of fine wire gauze above the flame and showed that the fire could not pass through it, although the burning vapour came up on one side and could be lit again on the other. The metal carries heat away so quickly that the gas below the gauze cools too much to burn, and this is the principle behind the safety lamp that Humphry Davy designed for coal miners. Faraday had once worked for Davy, and he spoke of the invention with evident pride.

Faraday lit a special lamp known as an Argand burner, which had a ring-shaped wick and a tall glass chimney, and the flame stood steady and bright without any flicker. The chimney caused a strong current of fresh air to rush up through the middle of the flame, bringing all the oxygen it needed. Without such a current, he explained, a flame is restless and unsteady, and it wastes much of its fuel.

Why does a flame stand up in a graceful tongue, rather than spreading out like a puddle of light? Because the hot gases around it are lighter than the cooler air, Faraday explained, and so they rise and carry the flame upward with them. On a spacecraft, where nothing rises, a candle flame is round instead, a small glowing ball.

What makes a candle flame so bright, when most burning gases give out little light of their own? Faraday's answer was that the flame is full of tiny particles of solid carbon, much too small to see, which are heated until they glow white-hot as they rise. A clear, colourless gas gives out hardly any light, but a cloud of glowing particles shines like a small sun.

To prove his point, Faraday held a cold white plate in the flame, and the surface of it soon became coated with a sooty black deposit. It was the very same carbon that had been glowing a moment earlier, caught and cooled before it could burn away. The audience could now see with their own eyes what the light of a candle is made of.

Some materials, such as camphor and turpentine, burn with a thick and smoky flame that sends up clouds of black soot. In these flames, Faraday explained, there is too much carbon for the air to burn, and so part of it escapes unburned and drifts away in a dark cloud. Anyone who has seen a smoking lamp in a draughty room has seen the same thing.

A good candle, by contrast, makes no smoke, for each glowing particle of carbon is burned away at the edge of the flame, where fresh air reaches it. What is left is not a solid at all but an invisible gas, which rises quietly into the room and disappears. Faraday found this a beautiful arrangement, since the candle first uses its carbon to make light and then uses it up completely.

Faraday lowered a glass jar over a burning candle, and for a few moments it went on burning as before, then it began to shrink and grow dim. Before long the flame died altogether, though there was still plenty of wax left on the wick. Something in the air, he concluded, had been used up, and a candle cannot burn without a continued supply of it.

Faraday compared two candles standing in two bottles, one open to the room and the other tightly closed, and the difference was plain to everyone. The first burned on cheerfully, while the second grew faint and was soon gone, which showed that burning depends on a steady supply of fresh air. The air in the closed bottle, once used, could not feed the flame any more.

In the second lecture Faraday filled a metal vessel with a freezing mixture of ice and salt and held it above a burning lamp. Before long the outside of the vessel was covered with a dew of tiny drops that ran together and fell, and when they were collected they proved to be plain water. The flame, it seemed, was making water out of nothing visible at all, which was both strange and delightful.

To be sure that the liquid was really water, Faraday used a test that no one could mistake: he dropped a small piece of the metal potassium into it. Potassium bursts into a lilac flame when it touches water, and it did so with the drops collected above the candle, exactly as it would have done with water from a tap. The candle, he could now say with confidence, was truly making water as it burned.

Faraday reminded his young listeners that ice, water and steam are three forms of one and the same substance, which changes its appearance only according to its warmth. Cooled enough, water becomes a hard solid, and heated enough, it becomes an invisible gas that fills far more space than the liquid did. The water from the candle, then, was nothing more mysterious than steam turned back to drops.

Faraday then connected a battery to two wires dipped in water, and tiny bubbles of gas began to rise from each, to be gathered in two glass tubes standing above them. One tube filled with exactly twice as much gas as the other, which showed that water is not a simple substance but a compound of two different things. The candle, it turned out, had been working on those same two things all along.

The gas that had filled the larger tube was hydrogen, which Faraday described as the lightest of all substances. He filled soap bubbles with it and sent them floating up towards the ceiling of the lecture hall, where ordinary bubbles, filled with air, would have slowly drifted down. It was a lesson in the lightness of a gas that nobody who watched it would easily forget.

When Faraday set light to the hydrogen, it burned with a pale and almost invisible flame that gave out hardly any light. There was no soot and no smoke, for hydrogen holds no carbon, and the only product of its burning was water, which gathered in drops on a cold vessel held above. It was a vivid lesson in how much a flame depends on what is burning inside it.

Faraday now revealed where the water of the candle comes from: the wax contains hydrogen, together with carbon, and as the wax burns the hydrogen is changed into water. The candle's flame is therefore a double fire, with the carbon glowing and giving light while the hydrogen quietly makes dew. Neither part, he said, can be seen in the solid wax, though both are there from the start.

Faraday turned in the next lecture to the second gas that water contains, which is oxygen. He made some by gently heating a mixture of two powders, chlorate of potash and manganese, in a small flask, and the gas bubbled through water into a jar where it could be saved. It was invisible, like air, but the audience was soon to see how very different it was.

When Faraday plunged a burning candle into a jar of pure oxygen, the flame flared up into a brilliant white blaze that dazzled the people in the front rows. A piece of charcoal, which in air only glows a dull red, glowed so fiercely in the gas that it seemed to be on fire all over. It was clear that oxygen was the part of the air that feeds a flame.

The air that surrounds us, Faraday told his listeners, is a mixture of several gases, and the oxygen in it makes up only about one fifth of the whole. This is the active part that supports burning and breathing, and it is mixed with a much larger share of another gas that is far less lively. Without the oxygen, a candle in a jar of air would never have burned at all.

Faraday went on to show that the air, which seems to be nothing at all, has weight, and that the whole depth of the atmosphere presses down on everything beneath it. The pressure at the surface of the Earth is about the weight of a kilogram on every square centimetre, a load we never notice because the air inside our bodies pushes back with equal force. It takes a pump and a sealed vessel to make this strange fact visible.

The greater part of the air, said Faraday, is nitrogen, a quiet and inactive gas that neither burns nor helps anything else to burn. He described it as a kind of gentle companion for the oxygen, since pure oxygen would make fires blaze so wildly that nothing could be kept safe. The nitrogen dilutes the oxygen and so tames it, which is a very useful thing for a world full of living creatures.

A burning candle makes a second product besides water, and Faraday found it by passing the gas from a flame through a jar of clear limewater. The water slowly turned cloudy and white, which is the sign of the gas now called carbon dioxide, and which he called carbonic acid in his own day. It is an invisible gas, and a flame makes it from the carbon in its fuel.

To show where the gas comes from, Faraday burned a piece of charcoal, which is almost pure carbon, in a jar of oxygen, and then shook limewater in the jar. It turned milky white just as it had done with the gas from the candle, which proved that the carbon of the candle becomes the same gas when it burns. Soot, charcoal and the black in a candle flame are all, in the end, one and the same substance.

This gas, Faraday showed, is heavier than air, and to prove it he poured it from one jar into another as if it were water. He also let it flow down a long trough over a row of burning candles, and one after another the flames went out as the invisible stream reached them. A candle, the audience could see, cannot burn in a gas that gives it no oxygen to feed on.

When a candle seems to burn away, nothing is really destroyed, for every part of the wax is changed into something else. The hydrogen becomes water vapour, the carbon becomes carbon dioxide, and both are invisible gases that rise into the room and mix with the air. A candle is not so much used up as moved from one place to another.

In the last lecture Faraday turned to carbon itself, in the form of charcoal, and asked his audience to notice that it burns in a very different way from wax. It glows a deep red and gives out great heat, but it makes no flame at all, because carbon does not first change into a vapour as the wax does. A flame, in other words, is nothing more than a burning gas, and charcoal shows that burning needs no flame.

To show how closely a candle resembles a lamp in the street, Faraday filled a small clay pipe with coal, sealed it with clay and set it in a fire. A gas soon came out of the stem, and when it was lit it burned with a bright flame, just as the vapour of a candle does. This was the very gas that lit the streets and houses of London in his day.

Faraday observed that the gas lamps along the London streets were, in principle, nothing but candles that took their fuel through a pipe rather than a wick. In each case a combustible gas is heated, burned in air and made to glow by particles of carbon, and in each case the products are water and carbon dioxide. Only the source of the fuel differs, and the chemistry is exactly the same.

Then Faraday did something that surprised the whole audience: he blew gently through a glass tube into clear limewater, and it clouded over and turned white, exactly as it had for the gas from a flame. The breath that leaves our bodies, in other words, contains the same invisible gas that a burning candle makes. It was a remarkable connection, and he let the children think about what it meant.

The explanation, said Faraday, is that the food we eat serves as a kind of fuel, and that the oxygen we breathe in combines with the carbon in it, deep within the body. The carbon dioxide that results is carried away by the blood and breathed out, so that every breath is a small act of burning. A candle burns the fuel it is given, and so, in a quiet way, do we.

It is this slow combustion, Faraday explained, that keeps our bodies warm, whatever the temperature outside. A candle burns quickly and with a bright flame, whereas the burning in a living body goes on gently and without any fire at all, yet both use the same fuel and air. The comparison between a person and a candle was, for many listeners, the greatest surprise of the whole series.

Faraday did not forget the green world, which takes in the carbon dioxide that candles and living animals send out into the air. Plants use the carbon to build their leaves and stems, and they return oxygen to the air, so that the substances flow round and round between living things and the atmosphere. The carbon that leaves one creature's breath may soon become part of a leaf.

What impressed Faraday most was that the same laws operate in a burning candle, in a growing plant and in a breathing child, and he wanted his young audience to understand that nature is one connected whole. A fire in the grate, a leaf in the sun and a heartbeat in the chest are all part of one great pattern of change. Once we understand a single small flame properly, he implied, we have taken the first step towards understanding everything.

Throughout the lectures Faraday urged his audience to look carefully, to ask questions and to test for themselves whatever they were told. A claim that cannot be checked by experiment, he implied, is not yet knowledge, however grand the person who makes it. He wanted them to leave the room not with a list of facts but with the habit of finding out.

One charm of the candle lectures is that many of the experiments can be repeated at home with very ordinary things, provided an adult is there to help with the flame. A plate held over a candle shows the soot, a jar lowered over it shows the need for air, and a cold glass held above it shows the dew. Fire is always dangerous, of course, and good scientists take care as well as notes.

Faraday was modest about all that he had shown, and he did not claim to have reached the end of the subject. A candle still had a great deal to teach, he said, and the lessons of these six lectures were no more than the first tentative steps, with much that nobody yet understood or explained. He hoped that some of the young people before him would one day carry the work much further than he had, and he looked forward to it.

At the close of the final lecture Faraday spoke directly to the children, and he expressed a wish that, when they grew up, they might be like candles. He hoped that each of them would shine as a light to those around them, and that every honest action of theirs would be as steady and as useful as a good flame. It was a gentle, modest ending to a most remarkable series of talks about a very small thing.

The lectures were published as a book in 1861, put together from notes taken at the lectures by a young scientist named William Crookes, and it has remained in print ever since. Teachers have used it for more than a century and a half, because it shows how to move from a simple observation to a deep idea in clear and easy steps. It is still among the most loved of all books about science, and it is easy to see why.

Faraday is remembered for far more than candles, for he also made discoveries about electricity and magnetism that helped to change the world. In 1831 he found that a moving magnet can produce an electric current in a coil of wire, which is the principle behind the electric generator and also, in reverse, the electric motor. Modern life, with its power stations and its machines, rests on a foundation that he helped to lay.

Perhaps the deepest lesson of the six lectures is that the smallest and most ordinary things can lead us to the largest ideas, provided we look at them carefully enough. A candle on a table opens the way to the study of air, water, heat, plants and the machinery of our own bodies. It is not the grandeur of the subject that matters, but the quality of the attention that we bring to it.

The next time you see a candle burning, look at it as Faraday taught his young audience to look, and notice the small cup of melted wax, the wick drawing up its fuel and the glowing particles of carbon. Think too of the water and the invisible gas rising into the room, and of the same quiet fire going on in your own body. A single flame, he showed, is a whole school of science held in the palm of the hand.
